claim: Cell migration requires the cyclical assembly and disassembly of focal adhesions.
source: Cell migration requires the cyclical assembly and disassembly of focal adhesions.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cell migration mechanisms.

claim: Adhesion induces phosphorylation of focal adhesion proteins, including Cas (Crk-associated substrate/p130Cas/BCAR1).
source: Adhesion induces phosphorylation of focal adhesion proteins, including Cas (Crk-associated substrate/p130Cas/BCAR1).
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Cas phosphorylation stimulates adhesion turnover.
source: However, Cas phosphorylation stimulates adhesion turnover.
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: SOCS6 and Cullin 5 are components of the CRL5SOCS6 ubiquitin ligase.
source: Here we show that suppressor of cytokine signaling 6 (SOCS6) and Cullin 5, two components of the CRL5SOCS6 ubiquitin ligase, inhibit Cas-dependent focal adhesion turnover at the front but not rear of migrating epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: SOCS6 and Cullin 5 inhibit Cas-dependent focal adhesion turnover at the front but not rear of migrating epithelial cells.
source: Here we show that suppressor of cytokine signaling 6 (SOCS6) and Cullin 5, two components of the CRL5SOCS6 ubiquitin ligase, inhibit Cas-dependent focal adhesion turnover at the front but not rear of migrating epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The front focal adhesions contain phospho-Cas which recruits SOCS6.
source: The front focal adhesions contain phospho-Cas which recruits SOCS6.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing colocalization and binding studies.

claim: If SOCS6 cannot access focal adhesions, adhesion disassembly is stimulated.
source: If SOCS6 cannot access focal adhesions, or if cullins or the proteasome are inhibited, adhesion disassembly is stimulated.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic experiments and inhibitor studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: If cullins are inhibited, adhesion disassembly is stimulated.
source: If SOCS6 cannot access focal adhesions, or if cullins or the proteasome are inhibited, adhesion disassembly is stimulated.
evidence: This is supported by MLN4924 inhibitor experiments.

claim: If the proteasome is inhibited, adhesion disassembly is stimulated.
source: If SOCS6 cannot access focal adhesions, or if cullins or the proteasome are inhibited, adhesion disassembly is stimulated.
evidence: This is supported by epoxomicin inhibitor experiments.

claim: The localized targeting of phospho-Cas within adhesions by CRL5SOCS6 and concurrent cullin and proteasome activity provide a negative feedback loop.
source: This suggests that the localized targeting of phospho-Cas within adhesions by CRL5SOCS6 and concurrent cullin and proteasome activity provide a negative feedback loop, ensuring that adhesion assembly predominates over disassembly at the leading edge.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Ubiquitination provides a new level of spatio-temporal control over cell migration.
source: By this mechanism, ubiquitination provides a new level of spatio-temporal control over cell migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Cells can attach to and pull on the ECM by using integrins.
source: Cells can attach to and pull on the ECM by using integrins ‒ transmembrane receptors that link ECM outside the cell to focal adhesions (FAs) and the actin cytoskeleton inside the cell (Alexander et al., 2008; Hynes, 2002; Pelham and Wang, 1997; Petrie et al., 2012; Puklin-Faucher and Sheetz, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Integrins are transmembrane receptors that link ECM outside the cell to focal adhesions and the actin cytoskeleton inside the cell.
source: Cells can attach to and pull on the ECM by using integrins ‒ transmembrane receptors that link ECM outside the cell to focal adhesions (FAs) and the actin cytoskeleton inside the cell (Alexander et al., 2008; Hynes, 2002; Pelham and Wang, 1997; Petrie et al., 2012; Puklin-Faucher and Sheetz, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: FAs are dynamic assemblies containing many proteins held together by dense networks of protein-protein interactions.
source: FAs are dynamic assemblies containing many proteins held together by dense networks of protein-protein interactions (Kanchanawong et al., 2010; Zaidel-Bar et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nascent FAs initiate when talin and other proteins associate with β integrin tails to stabilize an active integrin conformation and stimulate binding to the ECM.
source: Nascent FAs (often called focal complexes) initiate when talin and other proteins associate with β integrin tails to stabilize an active integrin conformation and stimulate binding to the ECM (Calderwood et al., 1999; Tadokoro et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Talin binds actin and vinculin.
source: Talin then binds actin and vinculin and actin flow exerts forces that create additional binding sites for vinculin, which in turn recruits more FA proteins and more actin (del Rio et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Actin flow exerts forces that create additional binding sites for vinculin.
source: Talin then binds actin and vinculin and actin flow exerts forces that create additional binding sites for vinculin, which in turn recruits more FA proteins and more actin (del Rio et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The force generated by actin flow, resisted by the ECM, creates a positive feedback loop to stabilize and grow the adhesion.
source: In this way, the force generated by actin flow, resisted by the ECM, creates a positive feedback loop to stabilize and grow the adhesion (Case and Waterman, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Force from the FA acts on actin filaments to induce the formation of contractile stress fibers and actin arcs.
source: In concert, force from the FA acts on actin filaments to induce the formation of contractile stress fibers and actin arcs (Burridge and Wittchen, 2013; Livne and Geiger, 2016; Roca-Cusachs et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The contraction of stress fibers and actin arcs provides motive power to advance the cell body.
source: The contraction of stress fibers and actin arcs provides motive power to advance the cell body.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell migration mechanisms.

claim: As the cell body moves forwards over an FA, the force vector is redirected and the FA remodels or disassembles.
source: As the cell body moves forwards over an FA, the force vector is redirected and the FA remodels or disassembles, allowing the FA proteins to recycle through the cytosol for reuse at the leading edge (Wehrle-Haller, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Inhibition of Rho kinase relaxes actomyosin tension and induces rapid FA disassembly.
source: Inhibition of Rho kinase or myosin relaxes actomyosin tension and induces rapid FA disassembly (Chrzanowska-Wodnicka and Burridge, 1996; Volberg et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Inhibition of myosin relaxes actomyosin tension and induces rapid FA disassembly.
source: Inhibition of Rho kinase or myosin relaxes actomyosin tension and induces rapid FA disassembly (Chrzanowska-Wodnicka and Burridge, 1996; Volberg et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ECM binding stimulates integrin-associated focal adhesion kinase (FAK) and Src-family kinases (SFKs).
source: ECM binding stimulates integrin-associated focal adhesion kinase (FAK) and Src-family kinases (SFKs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about integrin signaling.

claim: Tyrosine kinases phosphorylate several FA proteins, helping to build the FA by creating phosphotyrosine (pY) sites that bind to the SH2 domains of additional FA proteins.
source: These tyrosine kinases phosphorylate several FA proteins, helping to build the FA by creating phosphotyrosine (pY) sites that bind to the SH2 domains of additional FA proteins, as well as by activating RhoA (Parsons et al., 2010; Zaidel-Bar et al., 2003, 2007b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Tyrosine kinases help build the FA by activating RhoA.
source: These tyrosine kinases phosphorylate several FA proteins, helping to build the FA by creating phosphotyrosine (pY) sites that bind to the SH2 domains of additional FA proteins, as well as by activating RhoA (Parsons et al., 2010; Zaidel-Bar et al., 2003, 2007b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: FA size increases when endogenous SFKs are activated.
source: Thus, FA size increases when endogenous SFKs are activated, consistent with a positive role for SFKs during FA assembly (Thomas et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: FA size increases and FA turnover is inhibited in fibroblasts with mutations in Src, FAK, or a variety of Src/FAK substrates.
source: For example, FA size increases and FA turnover is inhibited in fibroblasts with mutations in Src, FAK, or a variety of Src/FAK substrates (Ilic et al., 1995; Ren et al., 2000; Volberg et al., 2001; Webb et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental work.

claim: FAs grow when kinase-inactive Src is over-expressed.
source: Furthermore, FAs grow when kinase-inactive Src is over-expressed (Fincham and Frame, 1998), and activated mutant Src weakens integrin-cytoskeletal interactions and accelerates FA disassembly (Felsenfeld et al., 1999; Fincham and Frame, 1998; Fincham et al., 1995; Galbraith et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Activated mutant Src weakens integrin-cytoskeletal interactions and accelerates FA disassembly.
source: Furthermore, FAs grow when kinase-inactive Src is over-expressed (Fincham and Frame, 1998), and activated mutant Src weakens integrin-cytoskeletal interactions and accelerates FA disassembly (Felsenfeld et al., 1999; Fincham and Frame, 1998; Fincham et al., 1995; Galbraith et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental work.

claim: Cas is an FA protein that is phosphorylated by Src when integrins engage the ECM.
source: Cas (p130Cas, BCAR1) is an FA protein that is phosphorylated by Src when integrins engage the ECM (Fonseca et al., 2004; Nojima et al., 1995; Petch et al., 1995; Vuori and Ruoslahti, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cell motility and invasion are stimulated when Cas is over-expressed.
source: Cell motility and invasion are stimulated when Cas is over-expressed and inhibited when Cas is deleted (Brabek et al., 2005; Cary et al., 1998; Honda et al., 1999, 1998; Huang et al., 2002; Patwardhan et al., 2006; Sanders and Basson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental work.

claim: Cell motility and invasion are inhibited when Cas is deleted.
source: Cell motility and invasion are stimulated when Cas is over-expressed and inhibited when Cas is deleted (Brabek et al., 2005; Cary et al., 1998; Honda et al., 1999, 1998; Huang et al., 2002; Patwardhan et al., 2006; Sanders and Basson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental work.

claim: Phosphorylation of Cas by SFKs induces binding to adaptor proteins Crk/CrkL.
source: At the molecular level, phosphorylation of Cas by SFKs induces binding to adaptor proteins Crk/CrkL and activation of the Rac1 and Rap1 GTPases (Hasegawa et al., 1996; Sakai et al., 1994; Tanaka et al., 1994; Vuori et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Phosphorylation of Cas by SFKs induces activation of the Rac1 and Rap1 GTPases.
source: At the molecular level, phosphorylation of Cas by SFKs induces binding to adaptor proteins Crk/CrkL and activation of the Rac1 and Rap1 GTPases (Hasegawa et al., 1996; Sakai et al., 1994; Tanaka et al., 1994; Vuori et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Forced relocalization of CrkL to FAs stimulates migration via DOCK1 and Rac1.
source: Forced relocalization of CrkL to FAs stimulates migration via DOCK1 and Rac1 (Li et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: A SFK/Cas pathway stimulates protrusive activity, inhibits stress fibers, and stimulates FA disassembly.
source: A SFK/Cas pathway stimulates protrusive activity, inhibits stress fibers, and stimulates FA disassembly (Webb et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Cas is mechanosensitive.
source: Interestingly, Cas is mechanosensitive.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citations in the text.

claim: Cytoskeletal tension induces Cas tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: Cytoskeletal tension induces Cas tyrosine phosphorylation (Janostiak et al., 2011; Tamada et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Mechanical extension of purified Cas promotes its phosphorylation by SFKs in vitro.
source: Mechanical extension of purified Cas promotes its phosphorylation by SFKs in vitro (Sawada et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: CRL5SOCS6 is a cullin-RING ubiquitin E3 ligase composed of cullin-5 (Cul5), Rbx2, elonginBC and suppressor of cytokine signaling 6 (SOCS6).
source: Here we provide evidence that CRL5SOCS6, a cullin-RING ubiquitin E3 ligase composed of cullin-5 (Cul5), Rbx2, elonginBC and suppressor of cytokine signaling 6 (SOCS6), inhibits pYCas-dependent FA turnover at the front of migrating epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: CRL5SOCS6 inhibits pYCas-dependent FA turnover at the front of migrating epithelial cells.
source: Here we provide evidence that CRL5SOCS6, a cullin-RING ubiquitin E3 ligase composed of cullin-5 (Cul5), Rbx2, elonginBC and suppressor of cytokine signaling 6 (SOCS6), inhibits pYCas-dependent FA turnover at the front of migrating epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: SOCS6 is recruited to pYCas in FAs at the leading edge.
source: We find that SOCS6 is recruited to pYCas in FAs at the leading edge, and that localization of SOCS6 to leading edge FAs slows their disassembly, dependent on cullin and proteasome activity and on binding of SOCS6 to Cas and CRL5.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Localization of SOCS6 to leading edge FAs slows their disassembly.
source: We find that SOCS6 is recruited to pYCas in FAs at the leading edge, and that localization of SOCS6 to leading edge FAs slows their disassembly, dependent on cullin and proteasome activity and on binding of SOCS6 to Cas and CRL5.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: SOCS6 slowing of FA disassembly is dependent on cullin activity.
source: We find that SOCS6 is recruited to pYCas in FAs at the leading edge, and that localization of SOCS6 to leading edge FAs slows their disassembly, dependent on cullin and proteasome activity and on binding of SOCS6 to Cas and CRL5.
evidence: This is supported by MLN4924 inhibitor experiments.

claim: SOCS6 slowing of FA disassembly is dependent on proteasome activity.
source: We find that SOCS6 is recruited to pYCas in FAs at the leading edge, and that localization of SOCS6 to leading edge FAs slows their disassembly, dependent on cullin and proteasome activity and on binding of SOCS6 to Cas and CRL5.
evidence: This is supported by epoxomicin inhibitor experiments.

claim: SOCS6 slowing of FA disassembly is dependent on binding of SOCS6 to Cas.
source: We find that SOCS6 is recruited to pYCas in FAs at the leading edge, and that localization of SOCS6 to leading edge FAs slows their disassembly, dependent on cullin and proteasome activity and on binding of SOCS6 to Cas and CRL5.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with SOCS6 mutants.

claim: SOCS6 slowing of FA disassembly is dependent on binding of SOCS6 to CRL5.
source: We find that SOCS6 is recruited to pYCas in FAs at the leading edge, and that localization of SOCS6 to leading edge FAs slows their disassembly, dependent on cullin and proteasome activity and on binding of SOCS6 to Cas and CRL5.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with SOCS6 mutants.

claim: SOCS6 is not present in adhesions under the cell body.
source: SOCS6 is not present in adhesions under the cell body, and sustained Cas signaling may facilitate their disassembly.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing differential localization.

claim: Sustained Cas signaling may facilitate disassembly of adhesions under the cell body.
source: SOCS6 is not present in adhesions under the cell body, and sustained Cas signaling may facilitate their disassembly.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data.

claim: CRL5SOCS6 targets pYCas within adhesions at the front of the cell.
source: The results suggest that CRL5SOCS6 targets pYCas within adhesions at the front of the cell, thereby allowing FAs to grow and provide anchorage for stress fibers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: Cul5 inhibits the epidermal growth factor (EGF)-independent migration of MCF10A epithelial cells.
source: We previously reported that Cul5 inhibits the epidermal growth factor (EGF)-independent migration of MCF10A epithelial cells (Teckchandani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a previously published finding cited from prior work.

claim: Cul5-depleted cells migrate considerably faster than control cells.
source: Cul5-depleted cells migrate considerably faster than control cells and have an exaggerated leading lamellipodium bearing tiny FAs, few stress fibers and dynamic membrane ruffles.
evidence: This is a previously published finding cited from prior work.

claim: Cul5-depleted cells have an exaggerated leading lamellipodium bearing tiny FAs, few stress fibers and dynamic membrane ruffles.
source: Cul5-depleted cells migrate considerably faster than control cells and have an exaggerated leading lamellipodium bearing tiny FAs, few stress fibers and dynamic membrane ruffles.
evidence: This is a previously published finding cited from prior work.

claim: The increased migration of Cul5-depleted cells requires Src.
source: The increased migration requires Src, suggesting that CRL5 may negatively regulate pY proteins.
evidence: This is a previously published finding cited from prior work.

claim: CRL5 targets pY proteins through the SH2 domains of SOCS substrate receptors.
source: CRL5 targets pY proteins through the SH2 domains of SOCS substrate receptors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRL5 mechanism.

claim: SOCS6 targets pYCas.
source: Knock-down experiments suggested that different SOCS proteins regulate different aspects of migration, with SOCS6 targeting pYCas and inhibiting ruffling.
evidence: This is a previously published finding cited from prior work.

claim: SOCS6 inhibits ruffling.
source: Knock-down experiments suggested that different SOCS proteins regulate different aspects of migration, with SOCS6 targeting pYCas and inhibiting ruffling.
evidence: This is a previously published finding cited from prior work.

claim: Migrating MCF10A cells contained large FAs and prominent stress fibers along the leading edge.
source: We previously noted that migrating MCF10A cells contained large FAs and prominent stress fibers along the leading edge, which were lost following Cul5 knockdown (Teckchandani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a previously published observation cited from prior work.

claim: Large FAs and prominent stress fibers along the leading edge were lost following Cul5 knockdown.
source: We previously noted that migrating MCF10A cells contained large FAs and prominent stress fibers along the leading edge, which were lost following Cul5 knockdown (Teckchandani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a previously published observation cited from prior work.

claim: TIRF microscopy of migrating EYFP-vinculin-expressing cells revealed large FAs at the cell front.
source: TIRF microscopy of migrating EYFP-vinculin-expressing cells also revealed large FAs at the cell front, but also detected many much smaller FAs all across the ventral surface (Figure 1a, left).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: TIRF microscopy of migrating EYFP-vinculin-expressing cells detected many much smaller FAs all across the ventral surface.
source: TIRF microscopy of migrating EYFP-vinculin-expressing cells also revealed large FAs at the cell front, but also detected many much smaller FAs all across the ventral surface (Figure 1a, left).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Large FAs were absent from migrating cells that had been treated with Cul5 siRNA.
source: Large FAs were absent from migrating cells that had been treated with Cul5 siRNA (Figure 1a, right, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1a for knockdown efficiency).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Approximately 3.6% of FAs at the front of control cells were larger than 200 pixels (5 µm2).
source: While the number of large FAs at the front of control cells was not sufficient to affect the mean or median FA size, approximately 3.6% of FAs at the front of control cells were larger than 200 pixels (5 µm2), but <0.5% of FAs at the front of Cul5-deficient cells were this large (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Less than 0.5% of FAs at the front of Cul5-deficient cells were larger than 200 pixels (5 µm2).
source: While the number of large FAs at the front of control cells was not sufficient to affect the mean or median FA size, approximately 3.6% of FAs at the front of control cells were larger than 200 pixels (5 µm2), but <0.5% of FAs at the front of Cul5-deficient cells were this large (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: FAs at the front of Cul5-deficient cells were notably more dynamic than those at the front of control cells.
source: FAs at the front of Cul5-deficient cells were notably more dynamic than those at the front of control cells (Video 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Many FAs at the front of control cells were present during the entire movie.
source: Many FAs at the front of control cells were white, indicating that they were present during the entire movie, while most FAs at the front of Cul5-deficient cells were singly colored, indicating they were short-lived.
evidence: This is based on color-coded time-lapse analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Most FAs at the front of Cul5-deficient cells were short-lived.
source: Many FAs at the front of control cells were white, indicating that they were present during the entire movie, while most FAs at the front of Cul5-deficient cells were singly colored, indicating they were short-lived.
evidence: This is based on color-coded time-lapse analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: FAs at the front and back of control cells assembled and disassembled with similar rate constants.
source: We found that FAs at the front and back of control cells assembled and disassembled with similar rate constants (0.012–0.013 min−1 for assembly; 0.008–0.009 min-1 for disassembly), suggesting that the front FAs were not larger because of increased assembly or decreased disassembly (Figure 1f, Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 1f and Table 1.

claim: There was no correlation between mean FA area and assembly or disassembly rate constants.
source: Indeed, there was no correlation between mean FA area and assembly or disassembly rate constants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), as expected for first-order reactions.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Removing Cul5 had no effect on the assembly or disassembly of back FAs.
source: Removing Cul5 had no effect on the assembly or disassembly of back FAs (Figure 1f, Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 1f and Table 1.

claim: Removing Cul5 stimulated both assembly and disassembly of front FAs approximately two-fold.
source: At the front, however, removing Cul5 stimulated both assembly and disassembly approximately two-fold, to ~0.029 min−1 for assembly and ~0.021 min−1 for disassembly (Figure 1f, Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 1f and Table 1.

claim: The percentage of FAs with disassembly rates <0.02 min−1 shifted from >60% to <10% when Cul5 was removed.
source: The increase in disassembly of leading edge FAs was also apparent from histograms of disassembly rate constants: the percentage of FAs with disassembly rates <0.02 min−1 shifted from >60% to <10% when Cul5 was removed (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Most large FAs at the front of control cells persisted for longer than the 3 hr duration of the movies.
source: While we were unable to directly measure the lifetimes of the large FAs at the front of control cells, most persisted for longer than the 3 hr duration of the movies, suggesting lifetimes exceeding 3 hr.
evidence: This is an observation from time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: Front FAs of Cul5-deficient cells had an average 24 min half time for assembly, 36 min stable phase, and 33 min half time for disassembly, for a total 93 min average lifetime.
source: In contrast, front FAs of Cul5-deficient cells had an average 24 min half time for assembly, 36 min stable phase, and 33 min half time for disassembly, for a total 93 min average lifetime.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The longer persistence of FAs at the front of control cells may contribute to their increased size.
source: The longer persistence of FAs at the front of control cells may contribute to their increased size.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Microtubules (MTs) are required for FA disassembly.
source: Microtubules (MTs) are required for FA disassembly and are observed repeatedly engaging with FAs during disassembly (Bershadsky et al., 1996; Kaverina et al., 1999, 1998; Stehbens et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: MTs are observed repeatedly engaging with FAs during disassembly.
source: Microtubules (MTs) are required for FA disassembly and are observed repeatedly engaging with FAs during disassembly (Bershadsky et al., 1996; Kaverina et al., 1999, 1998; Stehbens et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Nocodazole stabilized FAs in both control and Cul5-deficient cells.
source: We found that nocodazole stabilized FAs in both control and Cul5-deficient cells (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: FAs disappeared more rapidly from Cul5-deficient cells than control cells upon nocodazole removal.
source: However, FAs disappeared more rapidly from Cul5-deficient cells than control cells upon nocodazole removal (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Stress fibers disappeared more rapidly from Cul5-deficient cells upon nocodazole removal.
source: Stress fibers also disappeared more rapidly from Cul5-deficient cells (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Accelerated FA disassembly in Cul5-deficient cells was not due to faster MT regrowth after nocodazole removal.
source: Accelerated FA disassembly in Cul5-deficient cells was not due to faster MT regrowth after nocodazole removal because the MT cytoskeleton fully recovered in less than 15 min whether or not Cul5 was present (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: MT plus ends reached FAs in the ventral membrane within minutes of removing nocodazole.
source: Indeed, MT plus ends, tracked with fluorescent plus-end binding-protein EB1, reached FAs in the ventral membrane within minutes of removing nocodazole (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Cul5 slows the disassembly of FAs after MTs have regrown.
source: Therefore, Cul5 slows the disassembly of FAs after MTs have regrown, implying that Cul5 controls the speed of disassembly after MT targeting.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: MT targeting is reported to stimulate FA disassembly by clathrin-dependent integrin endocytosis.
source: MT targeting is reported to stimulate FA disassembly by clathrin-dependent integrin endocytosis (Ezratty et al., 2009; Ezratty et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Depleting clathrin heavy chains (CHC) strongly inhibited FA disassembly in control cells.
source: Accordingly, depleting clathrin heavy chains (CHC) strongly inhibited FA disassembly in control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: CHC depletion only partly inhibited the more rapid FA disassembly in Cul5-deficient cells.
source: However, CHC depletion only partly inhibited the more rapid FA disassembly in Cul5-deficient cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), suggesting that Cul5 inhibits a distinct mechanism of disassembly that is clathrin-independent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Clathrin-coated pits were missing from the leading lamellipodium of migrating Cul5-deficient cells.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, clathrin-coated pits were missing from the leading lamellipodium of migrating Cul5-deficient cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), as recently reported for other cell types (Kural et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Cul5 regulates FA disassembly through mechanisms unrelated to clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: This suggests that Cul5 regulates FA disassembly through mechanisms unrelated to clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: pYCas is required for FA disassembly in migrating fibroblasts.
source: Since we previously identified pYCas as a CRL5 substrate (Teckchandani et al., 2014) and since pYCas is required for FA disassembly in migrating fibroblasts (Webb et al., 2004), we tested whether Cul5-stimulated disassembly requires Cas.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Removing Cas suppressed the increase in FA disassembly at the front of migrating Cul5-deficient MCF10A cells.
source: We found that removing Cas suppressed the increase in FA disassembly at the front of migrating Cul5-deficient MCF10A cells but had no effect on FAs at the back or F control cells (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: Removing Cas had no effect on FAs at the back of migrating Cul5-deficient MCF10A cells.
source: We found that removing Cas suppressed the increase in FA disassembly at the front of migrating Cul5-deficient MCF10A cells but had no effect on FAs at the back or F control cells (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: Removing Cas had no effect on FAs in control cells.
source: We found that removing Cas suppressed the increase in FA disassembly at the front of migrating Cul5-deficient MCF10A cells but had no effect on FAs at the back or F control cells (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: Cas knockdown restored MT-dependent FA disassembly in Cul5-deficient HeLa cells in the nocodazole washout assay.
source: Consistent with a Cul5-Cas pathway, Cas knockdown restored MT-dependent FA disassembly in Cul5-deficient HeLa cells in the nocodazole washout assay, but had no effect on control cells (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: Cas knockdown had no effect on MT-dependent FA disassembly in control cells in the nocodazole washout assay.
source: Consistent with a Cul5-Cas pathway, Cas knockdown restored MT-dependent FA disassembly in Cul5-deficient HeLa cells in the nocodazole washout assay, but had no effect on control cells (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: Cas is required for increased FA disassembly when Cul5 is absent.
source: Therefore, Cas is required for increased FA disassembly when Cul5 is absent.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Removal of Cas suppressed the increased FA assembly of Cul5-deficient cells.
source: Removal of Cas also suppressed the increased FA assembly of Cul5-deficient cells (Figure 3a,b), consistent with the observation that FA and stress fiber assembly is slowed in cas mutant fibroblasts (Antoku et al., 2008; Honda et al., 1998), potentially due to decreased signaling through a Crk/ C3G/Rap1 signaling pathway (Li et al., 2002; Voss et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: FA and stress fiber assembly is slowed in cas mutant fibroblasts.
source: Removal of Cas also suppressed the increased FA assembly of Cul5-deficient cells (Figure 3a,b), consistent with the observation that FA and stress fiber assembly is slowed in cas mutant fibroblasts (Antoku et al., 2008; Honda et al., 1998), potentially due to decreased signaling through a Crk/ C3G/Rap1 signaling pathway (Li et al., 2002; Voss et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SOCS6 is the substrate receptor through which CRL5 binds pYCas.
source: SOCS6 is the substrate receptor through which CRL5 binds pYCas (Teckchandani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a previously published finding cited from prior work.

claim: Depleting SOCS6 stimulated FA disassembly at the front but not back of migrating MCF10A cells.
source: Accordingly, depleting SOCS6 stimulated FA disassembly at the front but not back of migrating MCF10A cells (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: SOCS6 depletion stimulated FA disassembly in the nocodazole washout assay.
source: SOCS6 depletion also stimulated FA disassembly in the nocodazole washout assay and Cas knockdown inhibited this effect (Figure 4c–e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c–e.

claim: Cas knockdown inhibited the effect of SOCS6 depletion on FA disassembly in the nocodazole washout assay.
source: SOCS6 depletion also stimulated FA disassembly in the nocodazole washout assay and Cas knockdown inhibited this effect (Figure 4c–e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c–e.

claim: Normal rates of FA disassembly were rescued by re-expression of wildtype SOCS6.
source: Normal rates of FA disassembly were rescued by re-expression of wildtype SOCS6, but not by mutant SOCS6LCQQ that cannot bind elongin B and the rest of the CRL5 complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Mutant SOCS6LCQQ that cannot bind elongin B and the rest of the CRL5 complex did not rescue normal rates of FA disassembly.
source: Normal rates of FA disassembly were rescued by re-expression of wildtype SOCS6, but not by mutant SOCS6LCQQ that cannot bind elongin B and the rest of the CRL5 complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Expression of CasFF, a mutant that does not bind SOCS6, stimulated FA disassembly regardless of the presence or absence of Cul5.
source: Moreover, expression of CasFF, a mutant that does not bind SOCS6 (Teckchandani et al., 2014), stimulated FA disassembly regardless of the presence or absence of Cul5, while wildtype Cas only stimulated FA disassembly when Cul5 was absent and Cas15F, a mutant that cannot signal downstream, did not stimulate FA disassembly even when Cul5 was absent (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Wildtype Cas only stimulated FA disassembly when Cul5 was absent.
source: Moreover, expression of CasFF, a mutant that does not bind SOCS6 (Teckchandani et al., 2014), stimulated FA disassembly regardless of the presence or absence of Cul5, while wildtype Cas only stimulated FA disassembly when Cul5 was absent and Cas15F, a mutant that cannot signal downstream, did not stimulate FA disassembly even when Cul5 was absent (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Cas15F, a mutant that cannot signal downstream, did not stimulate FA disassembly even when Cul5 was absent.
source: Moreover, expression of CasFF, a mutant that does not bind SOCS6 (Teckchandani et al., 2014), stimulated FA disassembly regardless of the presence or absence of Cul5, while wildtype Cas only stimulated FA disassembly when Cul5 was absent and Cas15F, a mutant that cannot signal downstream, did not stimulate FA disassembly even when Cul5 was absent (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b.

claim: SOCS6 inhibits FA disassembly dependent on binding to both Cas and CRL5.
source: These results suggest that SOCS6 inhibits FA disassembly dependent on binding to both Cas and CRL5.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Unlike Cul5, SOCS6 did not impact FA assembly rates.
source: However, unlike Cul5, SOCS6 did not impact FA assembly rates (Figure 4b), suggesting that, while an increase in pYCas (and other SOCS6 targets) is sufficient to stimulate disassembly, increased pYCas does not accelerate assembly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: An increase in pYCas is sufficient to stimulate disassembly.
source: However, unlike Cul5, SOCS6 did not impact FA assembly rates (Figure 4b), suggesting that, while an increase in pYCas (and other SOCS6 targets) is sufficient to stimulate disassembly, increased pYCas does not accelerate assembly.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data.

claim: Increased pYCas does not accelerate assembly.
source: However, unlike Cul5, SOCS6 did not impact FA assembly rates (Figure 4b), suggesting that, while an increase in pYCas (and other SOCS6 targets) is sufficient to stimulate disassembly, increased pYCas does not accelerate assembly.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data.

claim: Other SOCS proteins may target different pY substrates for ubiquitination by CRL5 to regulate FA assembly.
source: Other SOCS proteins may target different pY substrates for ubiquitination by CRL5 to regulate FA assembly.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: T7 epitope-tagged SOCS6 was enriched in FAs relative to the rest of the ventral membrane.
source: However, when we transiently transfected HeLa cells with T7 epitope-tagged SOCS6, the tagged protein was enriched in FAs relative to the rest of the ventral membrane (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: FA localization of SOCS6 was inhibited in cells treated with Cas siRNA.
source: FA localization of SOCS6 was inhibited in cells treated with Cas siRNA or with the SFK inhibitor SU6656 (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: FA localization of SOCS6 was inhibited in cells treated with the SFK inhibitor SU6656.
source: FA localization of SOCS6 was inhibited in cells treated with Cas siRNA or with the SFK inhibitor SU6656 (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: A point mutation in the phosphotyrosine-binding SH2 domain of SOCS6 inhibited binding to pYCas.
source: Moreover, a point mutation in the phosphotyrosine-binding SH2 domain of SOCS6 inhibited binding to pYCas (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a) and prevented FA localization (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a and Figure 5a.

claim: A point mutation in the phosphotyrosine-binding SH2 domain of SOCS6 prevented FA localization.
source: Moreover, a point mutation in the phosphotyrosine-binding SH2 domain of SOCS6 inhibited binding to pYCas (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a) and prevented FA localization (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: pYCas is required for SOCS6 localization to FAs.
source: Therefore, pYCas is required for SOCS6 localization to FAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: mChSOCS6WT was approximately 1.6-fold more abundant in FAs in the front 6 µm than FAs in the rest of the cell.
source: Under these conditions, mChSOCS6WT co-localized with vinculin in FAs (Figure 5b). Remarkably, mChSOCS6WT was approximately 1.6-fold more abundant in FAs in the front 6 µm than FAs in the rest of the cell.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The ratio of pYCas to vinculin was approximately 3-fold higher in FAs in the front 6 µm than back.
source: We tested whether leading edge FAs are also enriched for pYCas. The ratio of pYCas to vinculin was approximately 3-fold higher in FAs in the front 6 µm than back (Fonseca et al., 2004) (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: pYCas is enriched in FAs at the front of migrating cells.
source: These results suggest that pYCas is enriched in FAs at the front of migrating cells and that SOCS6 preferentially associates with these FAs, as expected if SOCS6 binds to pYCas.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: SOCS6 preferentially associates with FAs at the front of migrating cells.
source: These results suggest that pYCas is enriched in FAs at the front of migrating cells and that SOCS6 preferentially associates with these FAs, as expected if SOCS6 binds to pYCas.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Inhibition of SOCS6 or Cul5 expression slows Cas turnover, causing a 2–3-fold increase in the steady-state level of Cas.
source: Inhibition of SOCS6 or Cul5 expression slows Cas turnover, causing a 2–3-fold increase in the steady-state level of Cas (Teckchandani et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by previously published data and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Phosphorylated Cas levels in FAs increased approximately 3-fold when Cul5 expression was inhibited.
source: Accordingly, phosphorylated Cas levels in FAs increased approximately 3-fold when Cul5 expression was inhibited, especially in FAs in the front 6 µm of the cell (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cas exchanges rapidly between the cytosol and FAs.
source: Since Cas exchanges rapidly between the cytosol and FAs (Janostiak et al., 2011; Machiyama et al., 2014), the increase in pYCas in FAs could be secondary to the increased Cas in the cytosol.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: mChS6mito still bound to Cul5 and to Cas.
source: To this end, we constructed mChS6mito, a fusion of mCherry, SOCS6 and a sequence that targets the mitochondrial outer membrane (Bear et al., 2000). mChS6mito still bound to Cul5 and to Cas (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), but localized to mitochondria instead of FAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: mChS6mito localized to mitochondria instead of FAs.
source: To this end, we constructed mChS6mito, a fusion of mCherry, SOCS6 and a sequence that targets the mitochondrial outer membrane (Bear et al., 2000). mChS6mito still bound to Cul5 and to Cas (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), but localized to mitochondria instead of FAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: mChS6 rescued FA disassembly in SOCS6-depleted cells but mChS6mito did not.
source: In the nocodazole washout assay, mChS6 rescued FA disassembly in SOCS6-depleted cells but mChS6mito did not (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c.

claim: SOCS6 needs to access FAs in order to inhibit their disassembly.
source: These results suggested that SOCS6 needs to access FAs in order to inhibit their disassembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: In the dark, CRY2mChS6 co-localized with FAK in FAs.
source: In the dark, CRY2mChS6 co-localized with FAK in FAs (Figure 6b left).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: In the light, CRY2mChS6 co-localized with CIBNGFPmito at the mitochondria and was not detected in FAs.
source: In the light, however, CRY2mChS6 co-localized with CIBNGFPmito at the mitochondria and was not detected in FAs (Figure 6b right).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Light inhibits FA disassembly in cells expressing CRY2mChS6 and CIBNGFPmito.
source: The results showed that light inhibits FA disassembly (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: SOCS6 must have access to FAs during the disassembly process.
source: This implies that SOCS6 must have access to FAs during the disassembly process, and that the steady state level of Cas in the cytoplasm only plays a minor role.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The steady state level of Cas in the cytoplasm only plays a minor role in FA disassembly.
source: This implies that SOCS6 must have access to FAs during the disassembly process, and that the steady state level of Cas in the cytoplasm only plays a minor role.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the optogenetic experiments.

claim: MT-dependent FA disassembly was stimulated when MLN4924 was added an hour before and during 30 min of nocodazole removal.
source: MT-dependent FA disassembly was stimulated when MLN4924 was added an hour before and during 30 min of nocodazole removal (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: MT-dependent FA disassembly was stimulated when epoxomicin was added an hour before and during 30 min of nocodazole removal.
source: A similar result was obtained with epoxomicin, a proteasome inhibitor (Meng et al., 1999) (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: One or more CRLs and the proteasome need to be active during the disassembly process.
source: The results suggest that one or more CRLs and the proteasome need to be active during the disassembly process.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the inhibitor experiments.

claim: Two hours of treatment with MLN4924 increased FA assembly and disassembly rates at front but not back of migrating MCF10A cells.
source: Moreover, two hours of treatment with MLN4924 also increased FA assembly and disassembly rates at front but not back of migrating MCF10A cells (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7a,b.

claim: Short exposure to MLN4924 increased pYCas levels in front but not back FAs.
source: This short exposure to MLN4924 increased pYCas levels in front but not back FAs and had no effect on total Cas levels (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Short exposure to MLN4924 had no effect on total Cas levels.
source: This short exposure to MLN4924 increased pYCas levels in front but not back FAs and had no effect on total Cas levels (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The activities of Cullins and the proteasome are required during the process of FA disassembly.
source: Combined with the optogenetics results, we suggest that SOCS6 regulates FA turnover locally by direct interaction with pYCas in or near FAs, and not by binding to or altering the steady state concentration of Cas or other proteins in the cytosol.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: SOCS6 regulates FA turnover locally by direct interaction with pYCas in or near FAs.
source: Combined with the optogenetics results, we suggest that SOCS6 regulates FA turnover locally by direct interaction with pYCas in or near FAs, and not by binding to or altering the steady state concentration of Cas or other proteins in the cytosol.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The SFK-Cas pathway is required for the rapid FA turnover at the leading edge of epithelial cells in which CRL5SOCS6-dependent ubiquitination has been inhibited.
source: We found that the SFK-Cas pathway is also required for the rapid FA turnover at the leading edge of epithelial cells in which CRL5SOCS6-dependent ubiquitination has been inhibited.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Cas phosphorylation is greatest in the large FAs at the front of normal cells and around the edge of spreading cells.
source: We and others have observed that Cas phosphorylation is greatest in the large FAs at the front of normal cells and around the edge of spreading cells (Fonseca et al., 2004; Sawada et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' data and citations.

claim: Towards the rear, Cas is less highly phosphorylated, there is less SOCS6, and disassembly is slow regardless of SOCS6 or Cul5 activity.
source: Towards the rear, Cas is less highly phosphorylated, there is less SOCS6, and disassembly is slow regardless of SOCS6 or Cul5 activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The regulation of SOCS6 localization is critical for selective stabilization of FAs at the leading edge as cells migrate forwards.
source: This suggests that the regulation of SOCS6 localization is critical for selective stabilization of FAs at the leading edge as cells migrate forwards.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Inhibition of SOCS6-CRL5 did not induce FA disassembly in cells that lack MTs.
source: Inhibition of SOCS6-CRL5 did not induce FA disassembly in cells that lack MTs.
evidence: This is supported by the nocodazole experiments.

claim: MTs trigger disassembly by a pathway that is inhibited by SFKs and Cas.
source: This suggests that MTs trigger disassembly by a pathway that is inhibited by SFKs and Cas.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: MT-induced FA disassembly requires the MT motor kinesin-1.
source: MT-induced FA disassembly requires the MT motor kinesin-1, presumably to mediate anterograde traffic along MTs towards the FA (Krylyshkina et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: MTs deliver a protein complex including IQSEC1, an activator of the Arf6 small GTPase, to FAs.
source: Indeed, MTs deliver a protein complex including IQSEC1, an activator of the Arf6 small GTPase, to FAs (Yue et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Arf6, together with clathrin, dynein, and clathrin adaptors such as Dab2 and Numb, stimulates integrin β1 endocytosis and MT-dependent adhesion turnover in keratinocytes and HeLa cells.
source: Arf6, together with clathrin, dynein, and clathrin adaptors such as Dab2 and Numb, stimulates integrin β1 endocytosis and MT-dependent adhesion turnover in keratinocytes and HeLa cells (Chao et al., 2009; Ezratty et al., 2009; Ezratty et al., 2005; Nishimura et al., 2007; Yue et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: MTs are involved in weakening the integrin-ECM connection by delivering matrix metalloproteases to FAs.
source: MTs are also involved in weakening the integrin-ECM connection by delivering matrix metalloproteases to FAs (Stehbens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: MT-dependent integrin endocytosis is not involved in the SFK-Cas FA disassembly pathway.
source: However, our evidence suggests that MT-dependent integrin endocytosis is not involved in the SFK-Cas FA disassembly pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Clathrin-coated pits are absent from the ventral surface of the leading edge of motile glioblastoma cells.
source: Clathrin-coated pits are absent from the ventral surface of the leading edge of motile glioblastoma cells (Kural et al., 2015) and were absent from the long leading lamellipodium of Cul5-deficient MCF10A cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Clathrin knockdown inhibited the slow FA disassembly in normal HeLa cells but not the rapid FA disassembly in Cul5-deficient HeLa cells.
source: Moreover, clathrin knockdown inhibited the slow FA disassembly in normal HeLa cells but not the rapid FA disassembly in Cul5-deficient HeLa cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: RING protein XRNF185, which destabilizes paxillin via the proteasome, stimulates mesodermal cell migration during convergent extension in Xenopus embryos.
source: RING protein XRNF185, which destabilizes paxillin via the proteasome, stimulates mesodermal cell migration during convergent extension in Xenopus embryos (Iioka et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Paxillin ubiquitination is stimulated by ubiquitin ligase RNF5.
source: On the other hand, paxillin ubiquitination is also stimulated by ubiquitin ligase RNF5, but RNF5 does not induce paxillin degradation and it slows, rather than stimulates, cell migration (Didier et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: RNF5 does not induce paxillin degradation and it slows, rather than stimulates, cell migration.
source: On the other hand, paxillin ubiquitination is also stimulated by ubiquitin ligase RNF5, but RNF5 does not induce paxillin degradation and it slows, rather than stimulates, cell migration (Didier et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: TRIM5 stimulates paxillin turnover and increases FA disassembly.
source: Other authors reported that TRIM5 stimulates paxillin turnover and increases FA disassembly. This is the opposite of the effect of CRL5SOCS6 in inhibiting disassembly (Uchil et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Inhibiting autophagy slows FA assembly and disassembly and increases FA lifetime and size.
source: Inhibiting autophagy slows FA assembly and disassembly and increases FA lifetime and size.
evidence: This is established knowledge about autophagy's role in FA dynamics.

claim: An ATG cargo receptor, NBR1, recruits autophagosomes to FAs to stimulate FA disassembly.
source: While it is unclear how autophagy stimulates FA assembly, the evidence suggests that an ATG cargo receptor, NBR1, recruits autophagosomes to FAs to stimulate FA disassembly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about autophagy's role in FA dynamics.

claim: NBR1 contains a ubiquitin-binding domain.
source: Interestingly, NBR1 contains a ubiquitin-binding domain, suggesting that ubiquitination may localize NBR1 to FAs during disassembly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NBR1 structure.

claim: Ubiquitination may localize NBR1 to FAs during disassembly.
source: Interestingly, NBR1 contains a ubiquitin-binding domain, suggesting that ubiquitination may localize NBR1 to FAs during disassembly.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on NBR1's structure.

claim: Localized degradation of talin by the protease calpain triggers FA disassembly.
source: Localized degradation of talin by the protease calpain also triggers FA disassembly (Bhatt et al., 2002; Franco et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Calpain is an endopeptidase that creates specific cleavage products.
source: However, calpain is an endopeptidase that creates specific cleavage products, and the talin fragments remain in the FA and regulate FA stability (Huang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Talin fragments remain in the FA and regulate FA stability.
source: However, calpain is an endopeptidase that creates specific cleavage products, and the talin fragments remain in the FA and regulate FA stability (Huang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis typically requires translocation of the ubiquitinated protein into the proteasome.
source: In contrast, ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis typically requires translocation of the ubiquitinated protein into the proteasome (Ravid et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Most of the Cas in a FA exchanges with Cas from the cytosol with a very rapid (~20 s) rate constant.
source: It is known that most of the Cas in a FA exchanges with Cas from the cytosol with a very rapid (~20 s) rate constant (Janostiak et al., 2011; Machiyama et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Decreased SOCS6 expression has been associated with aggressive disease and increased metastasis in some cancers.
source: This mechanism may be important in some cancers, where decreased SOCS6 expression has been associated with aggressive disease and increased metastasis (Fang et al., 2015; Letellier et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.
